name: Ivan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Ferncombe, which is four hundred dairy goats for a cheese maker, plus barley and oilseed rape on two hundred hectares. The owner lives in the city and runs a property business, so I'm the one on site. Milking is at six and four, I've got three staff and two seasonal workers, and every Monday I send him a report with the numbers. I'm a numbers person, so I actually like that part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask it to tidy up the Monday report or spot something odd in the milk records, like a doe whose yield dropped twelve percent. But I check everything. I don't trust a thing I haven't seen with my own eyes in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a sensible outcome. A few useful tools, no great upheaval. I'm not one for big posts online, so I'd probably just say it over a pint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the job I have stays the job I have. That's fine by me. I'd keep using it for the reports and that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. We're planning to extend the kidding shed next year, roughly forty thousand, and that would still go ahead. I'd maybe push the owner on the price we get from the cheese maker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What actually keeps you up at night in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk price, the weather and staff. Getting good milkers is hard. My biggest risk isn't a robot, it's Luka going back home and nobody answering the advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Nadia, your partner, what would she make of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's a vet nurse, so she'd just be glad nothing changed. She reads more about AI than I do. She'd probably be a bit disappointed, actually.

S0.say: I'd say it was a sensible outcome, with a few useful tools and no great upheaval. I'd say that over a pint rather than online.
S0.think: I think the job I have stays the job I have, and that suits me. I'd keep using AI for the reports and nothing more.
S0.do: Goes ahead with the planned kidding shed extension of about forty thousand. Pushes the owner to negotiate a better price from the cheese maker.
S0.quote: My biggest risk isn't a robot, it's Luka going back home and nobody answering the advert.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan frames everything as numbers and risks, and AI barely makes his list. His real worries are staffing, especially losing his milker Luka, and the milk price. He checks every AI answer himself, which fits his steady, proof-first approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms have always taken on new machines, and this is just the next lot. I'd say people need training for it, and the owners should pay. That's fair on both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the owner would see robot milking as a line on a spreadsheet. He'd ask me to cost it, I'd cost it, and the numbers would probably say yes. Then I'm the man who wrote the business case for cutting two of my own staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the robot milking systems properly, once two or three farms nearby had run them for a year. I'd go and see them, ask what broke. Then I'd cost it honestly and try to keep the staff on other work, like the kids and the fieldwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about me so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd be kept on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Somebody has to be on site to deal with it when it goes wrong. An owner in the city can't fix a robot at two in the morning. So I think I'd stay, for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in that business case, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honest, I'd put both options in. If I fudge the numbers to save Luka's job, the owner will just hire a consultant who won't.

S1.say: I'd say farms have always taken on new machines and this is just the next lot. People need training for it, and the owners should pay for that.
S1.think: I think the owner would see robot milking as a line on a spreadsheet and ask me to cost it. I'd end up writing the business case for cutting two of my own staff.
S1.do: Learns robot milking systems once nearby farms have run them for a year and visits them to ask what broke. Costs the change honestly and tries to move staff onto other work.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for his staff than for himself.
S1.quote: If I fudge the numbers to save Luka's job, the owner will just hire a consultant who won't.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan's discomfort is moral: he'd be writing the case that cuts his own workers. He insists he'd present the numbers honestly because fudging them would just bring in a consultant. He expects to keep his own job as the person on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and that the government and the big firms both need to slow down the rollout or pay for the gap. I'm not usually one to say that. But two years is not a plan, it's a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the owner keeps me longest, as the person who watches the machines. Then one day he asks why he needs that either. I'd have maybe a year more than my staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away, we were looking at a new car, that's gone. I'd try to get every month's spare into savings, from about four months to six. And I'd volunteer to run the robot system myself, so I'm the last person they'd let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Clear head, but a knot in the stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning change about how you'd handle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything gets rushed. You buy the first robot that's available, not the best one. With two years, I'd be signing off machines I haven't seen working, and that's against everything I believe about farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luka?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard to say it out loud. I'd tell him I'm sorry and I'd give him the best reference I've ever written. He's been here since he was twenty.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and that the government and big firms both need to slow the rollout or pay for the gap. I'm not usually one to say that, but two years is a crash, not a plan.
S2.think: I think the owner keeps me longest as the person who watches the machines, and then eventually asks why he needs that too. I'd likely have about a year more than my staff.
S2.do: Drops plans for a new car and puts every spare month's money into savings, aiming to move from four to six months. Volunteers to run the robot system himself so he is the last to be let go.
S2.feel: Anxious, clear-headed but with a knot in the stomach.
S2.quote: With two years, I'd be signing off machines I haven't seen working, and that's against everything I believe about farming.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fast picture Ivan stays measured, but he admits he'd be buying machines unseen, which goes against his core belief. He positions himself to be last out by running the robots. His sorrow is for Luka, his longest-serving worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and farms should use it. Train people now, while they still have jobs. I'd say that to the owner in the Monday report, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can choose, rather than be chosen. I'd still lose the job in the end, I think. But I'd be 32 with something else on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time farm business management course, evenings, maybe two years. I'd keep learning the robot systems as they come in. And I'd save towards six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. More like I've got homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between two years and five for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between a crash and a planned exit. Two years I'd be a passenger; five years I'd at least be driving. I'd still be scared, just busier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you'll be doing in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably managing more than one farm, or advising owners like mine. Owners still need someone to trust, even if it's someone who mostly reads screens. I don't know, though.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so farms should train people now while they still have jobs. I'd even say it to the owner in the Monday report.
S3.think: I think five years lets me choose rather than be chosen. I'd probably still lose this job in the end, but I'd be 32 with something else on my CV.
S3.do: Starts a part-time evening course in farm business management over about two years. Keeps learning the robot systems as they arrive and saves towards six months of cushion.
S3.feel: Still anxious, but it feels more like homework than a threat.
S3.quote: Two years I'd be a passenger; five years I'd at least be driving.
S3.fieldNote: For Ivan, time turns him from passenger to driver, and he picks a sober, practical course. He imagines a future as an advisor or multi-farm manager but doesn't overclaim it. He'd even put the warning into his weekly report to the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do this properly, and there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. I'd say it in the pub and at the farmers' discussion group. Calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to plan around. I'd be 37, Nadia and I would have kids by then, probably. It's not great news, but it's news I can put in a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the business course, then something on robotics servicing, maybe. I'd keep saving. And Nadia and I would get married next year like we planned, not put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm still not sure what the end looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying it's the same end point. Does the time really make you feel better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's fair. Even a planned exit is still an exit. I'm good at making plans, but I can't make a plan for a world where nobody needs a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the mistake you'd most want to avoid with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rush the first robot. Every farm that rushes it loses a season of milk. With ten years I'd want to be the second farm in the area to do it, not the first.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is time to do this properly, so nobody has an excuse for being caught out. I'd say it calmly in the pub and at the farmers' discussion group.
S4.think: I think ten years is enough to plan around, and I'd be 37 and probably have children by then. It's not good news, but it's news I can put into a plan.
S4.do: Takes the farm business course and then perhaps training in servicing robots, while saving steadily. Goes ahead with marrying Nadia next year as planned.
S4.feel: Uneasy, because he still can't picture the end.
S4.quote: I'm good at making plans, but I can't make a plan for a world where nobody needs a manager.
S4.fieldNote: Ivan's comfort comes from planning, and he admits he can't plan for a world with no managers. He wants to be the second farm to adopt, never the first, which captures his steady nature. He refuses to let the change delay his wedding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to test anything, and I'd be buying and firing in the same month. What would help is a rule on notice, so owners have to tell staff a year ahead, and help paying for courses while you're still working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the owners who never come. The owner has seen this farm twice in three years, and he'll see the robots' numbers every Monday. That distance is what worries me, more than the machines.

headlineQuote: The owner has seen this farm twice in three years, and he'll see the robots' numbers every Monday.
portrait: Ivan Rahman, 27, manages Ferncombe, a 400-goat dairy and arable farm for an owner who lives in the city, and sends him a numbers report every Monday. He's measured and proof-first, uses AI now and then and checks every answer. In steady change his worry is having to write the business case that cuts his own staff, especially his milker Luka. The two-year picture makes him anxious but not panicked, and with five or ten years he plans a business course, steady saving and his wedding to Nadia.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have to buy machines he hasn't seen working and let staff go in the same month.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that owners give staff a year's notice, and help paying for courses while people are still in work.
